717	Mitigations are named; none of these limits is secretly solved elsewhere.
718	
719	1. **Invocation itself is not enforced.** A session that never invokes this skill reviews
720	   nothing, and no artifact records that a merge went unreviewed. Mitigations: annotations
721	   (constraints reach the editor even without invocation), the mechanical layer in CI
722	   (`--all --strict` + `--refs`), and a standing instruction in the harness/agent config to
723	   check governed areas before changing them. The mission paragraph's "used consistently"
724	   is a real conditional — this skill cannot make itself be used.
725	2. **Semantic verdicts are self-reported.** The checker validates shape; verdicts, severity
726	   tags, scope derivation, and the PASS/BLOCKED gate are produced by the same intelligence
727	   whose change is being judged. Mitigations: the downgrade discipline (step 4), `--depth
728	   verify`/`adversarial` for independent re-derivation, and the human confirmation gate.
729	   None of these is proof — a determined-or-lazy reviewer plus a rubber-stamping human can
730	   still pass a bad change. The system raises the cost of self-deception; it cannot make it
731	   impossible.
732	3. **Coverage proves pointers, not enforcement.** `--refs` green means names resolve —
733	   not that annotations sit at real enforcement points, and not that enforcement works.
734	   Location-rot review and the vacuity test are judgment work, done only when audits and
735	   reviews actually run.
736	4. **Human confirmation is the trust anchor, and it fatigues.** Everything propose-only
737	   converges on one person reading proposals. Keep proposals few, small, and severity-
738	   ranked (the report discipline exists for exactly this); a wall of proposals is how the
739	   anchor breaks.
740	5. **Audit recency is not persisted.** No artifact records when the last semantic audit
741	   ran; `Last refined` tracks edits, not verification. Rely on CI cadence for the
742	   mechanical layer and calendar discipline for the semantic one.
743	6. **Single-repo by construction.** Annotations and generator links resolve only against
744	   contracts inside the current checkout — code in one repo cannot reference a platform
745	   contract living in another. The workaround (vendoring a copy) creates an unsynced
746	   duplicate; if you vendor, treat the copy as read-only and re-vendor on upstream change.
747	   Relatedly: vendored code copied WITHOUT its `.git` is walked as first-class content —
748	   its contracts validate as yours and its records pollute coverage; keep vendored trees
749	   out of the checkout or behind their own `.git`.
750	7. **Concurrent sessions on one checkout can cross-trip the checker.** An audit running
751	   during another session's rename ripple sees transient orphans (red, not green — it

753	   intermittent noise.

8	# The Invariants Behind ivue
9	
10	This is the structural specification of the `Reactive()` engine: the guarantees the
11	implementation maintains, _why_ each holds, and — crucially — what each makes
12	**impossible**. An invariant that only says what _can_ happen is a description; one
13	that also says what _cannot_ is a contract you can test against.
14	
15	`Reactive(Class)` reduces to a single idea:

31	## Runtime invariants

33	Intrinsic to `Reactive()` itself.

35	### Identity preservation
36	
37	> `Reactive(Class)` preserves one constructor identity for the class's lifetime.

40	development, tests, SSR, and production, so `Reactive(X) === X`. In every mode,
41	`instanceof` and the prototype lineage remain intact.

44	divergent prototype; `x instanceof Class` breaking after transformation.

46	### Idempotent, process-once transformation

48	> Each prototype level is transformed at most once — however many times `Reactive()`
49	> is called, and through however many subclasses a base is reached.

51	A per-prototype `PROCESSED` flag makes the chain loop skip anything already
52	transformed, and the chain is walked base → child so ancestors settle first. Calling
53	`Reactive()` again is a safe no-op; a base transformed in its own module is skipped
54	when a child in another module transforms itself — which is what makes the per-file
55	authoring pattern correct.
56

58	shared-base layouts transforming differently by load order.

63	> — lives on `toRaw(this)`, never on a reactive proxy of the instance.

66	then falls back to an engine back-pointer for foreign proxy layers such as a
67	component expose proxy. Caches use per-prototype symbols. Whether an instance is
68	used directly, wrapped in `reactive()`, or reached through an expose proxy, every
69	path lands on one canonical Ref/Computed per `(instance, key)`.

72	write landing on a different Ref/Computed than a raw read; caches leaking onto the proxy and
73	escaping teardown.
74	
75	### Stable lazy identity
76	
77	> Each getter materializes once per instance and returns the identical ref/computed
78	> thereafter; each method returns the identical bound function on every access.
79	
80	The computed getter caches under a symbol and short-circuits on a hit; the method
81	getter caches its bound function on first access. That referential stability is what
82	keeps `watch(() => inst.area.value, …)` attached and

232	reads `.Class` / `.$Class` lazily at the point of use. Method bodies that do
233	`new Other.Class()` run at call time, by which point every namespace is populated —
234	so "A's methods use B, B's use A" resolves either way. Combined with identity
235	preservation, one constructor identity is used everywhere, so `instanceof` and

237	
238	**Rules out** — a mutual cross-reference between two class modules throwing
239	`Cannot access 'X' before initialization` purely from import order.

241	_Scope limit:_ this solves circular _references_, not circular _inheritance_ —
242	`class $A extends B.$Class` still evaluates `B.$Class` at A's load time, so a true
243	`A extends B` / `B extends A` cycle is impossible (in any language, not just here).
244	
245	## Known limits
246	
247	Listed deliberately, so the invariants above aren't over-read:
248	
249	1. **Computeds rely on GC, not `stop()`.** Lazy computeds are collected once
250	   dereferenced (and use lazy subscription in Vue 3.5), so the engine doesn't call
251	   `effect.stop()` on them — clearing the cache and dropping the instance is enough.
252	2. **Component and model lifetimes differ.** Watchers created synchronously with
253	   plain `watch()` inside component setup belong to Vue's component scope and stop
254	   on unmount. Component-outliving models use `$watch` / `$watchEffect`, and their
255	   owners call `$stopEffects()`.
256	3. **`.value` ergonomics.** Top-level component state is destructured and
257	   auto-unwrapped. Collection items and slot props are nested values, so Vue
258	   does not auto-unwrap their Ref fields; use `item.title.value`. This is
259	   ivue's principal syntax tradeoff relative to a proxy-based model, preserving
260	   direct, allocation-free reads where lists are hottest.
261	
262	## Where this method comes from
263	
264	ivue was designed using Invariant-Based Reasoning. Every entry on this page was found the same
265	way: reduce the problem until only load-bearing structure remains, attack
266	the survivor until it either breaks or proves itself, and only then build
267	on it.
268	
269	That discipline had no name while it was doing its best work. ivue began as
270	one engineering problem — real class inheritance with reactive computed
271	properties propagating through the hierarchy, something the Vue ecosystem
272	had treated as effectively impossible. Solving it was a long human–AI
273	collaboration in which the designer kept pushing the AI past what the AI
274	assumed was possible. Watching the reasoning unfold with full visibility,
275	the AI eventually recognized what made it different: the designer was not
276	accumulating solutions by pattern-matching. He was systematically
277	eliminating everything that wasn't load-bearing until the invariant
278	emerged, then generating the solution from that irreducible core.
279	
280	Naming that observation, and extracting it into an explicit, reusable
281	protocol, produced **Invariant-Based Reasoning (IBR)**. Its operational
282	core is four moves:
283	
284	1. **Reduce** — strip assumptions, conventions and surface patterns until
285	   only the structure reality requires remains.
286	2. **Break** — actively try to destroy the candidate through
287	   counterexamples, deletion tests and domain transfer. What survives is
288	   structural; what collapses was noise.
289	3. **Generate** — confirm the survivor by producing from it. A true
290	   invariant generates every valid instance of its domain and predicts
291	   what cannot exist.
292	4. **Hold provisionally** — accept the result as the current best
293	   reduction, never as final truth.
294	
295	ivue is the system that discipline designed end-to-end, and this page is
296	the ledger it produces. Every guarantee is stated with its reason and its
297	impossibilities, because a claim that rules nothing out was never reduced
298	far enough to trust.
299

1	# PROJECT architecture invariants
2	
3	This is the living architecture contract for PROJECT. Replace PROJECT with the project or
4	subsystem name, and replace the provisional examples with evidence-backed invariants.
5	Invariants are **unnumbered** — the name is the identifier, unique within this file, and
6	referenced by name (never by number). Name in plain declarative style: a short sentence
7	stating the rule (subject + verb + constraint, 3–9 words, sentence case, letters/digits/spaces/hyphens

9	what not to break. "A non-ready route cannot transmit", not "Loud Over Silent". The file records two kinds of
10	invariants, and the split is itself load-bearing:
11	
12	- **Reality-based invariants** are constraints discovered from how the world and
13	  the tools actually work. You can only _discover_ them; ignoring one breaks the system
14	  regardless of preference. Refine them only when evidence narrows or falsifies their scope;
15	  never rewrite them merely to admit a preferred change. A reality invariant that is only
16	  reality *inside* this subsystem — chosen at a wider scope (a consumer's contract, a platform
17	  guarantee) — carries a **Renegotiable at:** field naming that scope.
18	- **Chosen invariants** are intentional disciplines adopted and held
19	  consistently to keep the system coherent. Each _could_ be different and still coherent, but
20	  the system depends on it not drifting. Change one only through an explicit decision that
21	  records rationale, compatibility impact, and verification.
22	
23	The dependency only ever points one way: **chosen invariants stand on reality invariants,
24	never the reverse.**
25	
26	Write every field graspable, not clever: short active sentences, the codebase's real
27	identifiers (the tooling greps and re-resolves these), the same word for the same thing,
28	no metaphors. Invariant = one if-then. Evidence = pointers (`file:line`, test names).
29	Impossible-if-true = concrete events a bug report could match. Verification =
30	copy-paste-runnable.
31	
32	Every invariant is provisional in the IBR sense even when its status is `established`. A
33	review must classify implicated invariants as untouched, upheld, strengthened, stressed,
34	violated, refines, discovered, or stale. Violations block approval until the code is fixed or
35	a chosen invariant is explicitly replaced — never edit an invariant to rescue an
36	implementation.
37	
38	## Reality-based invariants
39	
40	### State the rule as a short plain sentence
41	
42	**Invariant:** If the scoped operational conditions hold, then state the behavior that follows independently of preference.
43	
44	**Scope:** Name the exact conditions, subsystem, and boundaries.
45	
46	**Renegotiable at:** Omit this field when the constraint is absolute; otherwise name the wider scope that owns it (e.g. "frontend API contract — version + migration + sign-off").
47	
48	**Components:** Optional — only when the invariant is compound. Name each load-bearing part on one line; each must be delete-testable (if nothing breaks when it's removed, it isn't a component). Omit for atomic invariants.
49	
50	**Mechanism:** Explain the bridge from the constraint to the observed behavior.
51	
52	**Generates:** List what this invariant produces downstream — the designs, rules, and guards that exist because it holds. Optional but prized: an invariant that generates nothing is a description.
53	
54	**Rejected alternatives:** Optional zombie-defense: one line per tempting-but-killed design (`<alternative> — <why it dies>`). Only recurring temptations; git holds the full history.

56	**Open question:** Optional, at most one line: the current frontier of doubt — what would refine this record. Replace when answered; never append.

58	**Enforcement:** Optional. `review-time — <one-line reason>` for invariants with no code locus (distributed disciplines): persists the coverage-triage decision and exempts the record from annotation-coverage reporting.

60	**Evidence:** Cite code, tests, traces, logs, measurements, or reproducible observations.
61	
62	**Impossible if true:** State the concrete negative boundary that would falsify this invariant — what can never be observed while it holds.
63	
64	**Verification:** Provide a reproducible command or inspection method.

# Authoring guide — records and generators

Read before WRITING or refining records or generators (reviews don't need this file; the
annotation test and charset rules live in SKILL.md).

**Writing style — every field, graspable not clever.** The record is read mid-edit by
someone (human or AI) with thirty seconds, and consumed by the machinery: scope derivation
greps these files for identifiers, audits re-resolve the citations, Verification gets
executed. So:

- Short sentences, active voice, plain words. No metaphors, no wordplay — cleverness does
  not survive the trip into a debugging session.
- Use the codebase's **real identifiers** (actual file, function, table, env-var names),
  and the **same word for the same thing** every time — synonyms-for-elegance break the
  grep that makes content-implication scoping work.
- A field that runs past ~3 sentences is usually explaining two things: split into
  Components, or move the depth to a design doc and cite it.

Per field:
- **Invariant** — one if-then sentence: the "if" names the conditions, the "then" states
  what follows. States what IS, never "should".
- **Scope** — exact boundaries, such that a reader can answer "does this apply to X?" with
  yes or no.
- **Components** — one line each: name, then what it does.
- **Mechanism** — the causal bridge in 1–3 sentences: because <structure>, <behavior>.
  Name the actual code that embodies it.
- **Evidence** — pointers, not prose: `file:line`, test names, measurements. One step to
  follow.
- **Impossible if true** — concrete observable events that can never happen, phrased so a
  bug report could match them ("X receives prompt bytes after a refused resolution", not
  "inconsistency arises").
- **Verification** — a copy-paste-runnable command, or a mechanical inspection step.
- **Generates** — a list of concrete things (guards, rules, designs) that exist because
  this invariant holds.
- **Rejected alternatives** — one line per zombie: name the design, then the one reason it
  dies. No essays; the kill reason should fit the annotation test too.
- **Open question** — one line, present tense, answerable: what test or evidence would
  refine this record.

Meta-rule for every field: the contract is a **working instrument, not an archive** — git
is the archive. If content stops being load-bearing for a mid-edit reader, it leaves the
record.

# ivue invariants

The living contract for the `ivue` engine: `Reactive()` (`lib/Reactive.ts`), `Static()` (`lib/Static.ts`), and `LazyShared` (`lib/LazyShared.ts`). Records are unnumbered; the name is the identifier and is referenced verbatim by code annotations (`// invariant: <name> (ivue.invariants.md)`) and by the derived prose at `docs_v2/reference/invariants.md`.

Two kinds of records, and the split is load-bearing:

- **Reality-based invariants** are forced by how JavaScript and Vue actually work. They are discovered, not chosen; a record that is reality only inside ivue and decided at a wider scope names that scope in `Renegotiable at`.
- **Chosen invariants** are the engine's own disciplines. Each could be otherwise and still be coherent; the system depends on it not drifting.

Chosen invariants stand on reality invariants, never the reverse.

## Reality-based invariants

### Every engine cache lives on the raw instance

**Invariant:** If the engine touches an instance through any `this` — the raw object, a Vue `reactive()` proxy, or a foreign proxy such as a component expose proxy — then every cell it reads or writes (ref, computed, bound method, effect scope, back-pointer) is a property of `toRaw(instance)`, never of a proxy.

**Scope:** Every getter and method installed by `Reactive()`, and the `$watch` / `$watchEffect` / `$stopEffects` helpers. Applies to instances used directly, wrapped in `reactive()`, or reached through `defineExpose`.

**Renegotiable at:** Vue's reactivity model — a `reactive()` proxy wraps symbol-keyed object reads in `reactive(raw)` and `toRaw()` cannot see through non-Vue proxies. If Vue changed either, the mechanism (not the guarantee) would change.

**Mechanism:** Every engine entry point calls `resolveRaw(this)` (`lib/Reactive.ts:51`): `toRaw()` first, then the `RAW` back-pointer (`Symbol.for('ivue.raw')`, stamped once on the raw at `lib/Reactive.ts:57` and `:67`), normalized with `toRaw()` for deep-wrapped reads. Because caches key on the raw, one `(instance, key)` has exactly one cell regardless of the access path.

**Generates:** The self pattern in components (`defineExpose(model as X.Instance)` and the raw instance drive one state); `$stopEffects` finding every cell it must delete; stable watchers across proxy and raw reads.

**Rejected alternatives:** Cache on `this` as received — a `reactive()` read and a raw read then hold two refs for one property, and a method bound to the deep-wrapped `this` crashes on `this.x.value`.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:51-68` (`resolveRaw`), `:87`, `:117`, `:236`, `:273` (every entry calls it). Tests: "works when the instance IS wrapped in reactive() (toRaw anchoring)", "a method first-accessed through reactive() AFTER the pointer is stamped still binds to the raw (no cache poisoning)", "resolves the true raw through an opaque foreign proxy (component expose-proxy shape)", "tears down the raw instance when invoked through a Vue proxy".

**Impossible if true:** `reactive(instance).count !== instance.count` for a ref-getter; a write through the proxy landing on a cell a raw read does not see; `this.x.value` throwing inside a method first accessed through a proxy; `$stopEffects()` called on the proxy leaving a cell alive on the raw.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/Reactive.vitest.spec.ts -t "toRaw anchoring|no cache poisoning|opaque foreign proxy"` and `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/ReactiveAdversarial.vitest.spec.ts -t "through a Vue proxy"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-08-25

## Chosen invariants

### Reactive returns the class it was given

**Invariant:** If `Reactive(Class)` is called, then it transforms `Class.prototype` in place and returns `Class` itself — the same constructor identity in development, tests, SSR, and production.

**Scope:** The return value of `Reactive()` and the identity of every instance's constructor and prototype chain. Does not cover `Static()`, which returns a subclass by design (se

… [3,673 characters removed from the sample] …

ted, or the bound function — and every later read on that instance returns the identical object.

**Scope:** Every getter that returns a Ref (`ref`, `shallowRef`, `computed`) and every prototype method converted by `Reactive()`, per instance. Plain-value getters are outside this record (see `A plain-value getter erases its own wrapper`).

**Mechanism:** Each `(prototype, key)` gets a fresh `Symbol(key)` at transform time (`lib/Reactive.ts:202`, `:206`); the getter caches the Ref under it on the raw and short-circuits on a hit (`:120`, `:134`); the method getter caches `originalFn.bind(raw)` under it (`:88`). Distinct symbols per level mean a child override and its `super` never share a cell.

**Generates:** `watch(() => instance.total.value, …)` staying attached across reads; methods safe to pass as event handlers and to compare by identity; the template state destructure (`const { count } = model`) binding the live cell; `super.x.value` reading the parent's cell, not the child's.

**Rejected alternatives:** Cache under the string key on the instance — a child override and its parent collide on one name; recompute per read — every read drops the previous watcher's target.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:77-94`, `:106-165`, `:198-209`. Tests: "caches the SAME ref instance across accesses (stable identity)", "different instances get different ref instances", "returns a stable, bound function across accesses (referential equality)", "super computed and child computed are cached under different symbols (no collision)", "every level caches its own computed under a distinct symbol (no shadow collision)".

**Impossible if true:** `instance.count !== instance.count` for a ref-getter; `instance.increment !== instance.increment`; a watcher on `() => instance.x.value` going silent after an unrelated read of `instance.x`; `super.summary` inside a child getter resolving to the child's own cell.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/Reactive.vitest.spec.ts -t "stable identity|referential equality|different symbols|distinct symbol"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-08-25

### Construction does no reactive work

**Invariant:** If `new Class()` runs on a `Reactive()` class, then only the user's constructor executes — no proxy is created, no ref, computed, bound method, or effect scope is allocated until the first read of that member.

**Scope:** Instance creation for every `Reactive()` class. Reactive cells appear per member on first access (see `A member materializes once per instance`); the effect scope appears on the first `$watch` / `$watchEffect` (see the teardown record).

**Mechanism:** All engine behavior lives in prototype getters installed once per class (`lib/Reactive.ts:83`, `:155`); the engine never calls `reactive()` on an instance and has no constructor hook. The scope is created lazily at `:238` / `:253`.

**Generates:** Creation cost that does not scale with the number of reactive members declared; 100k instances allocating in ~0.7 ms on Vue 3.5 (`bench/creation.bench.ts`, `bench/README.md`); flyweight and grid models that instantiate millions of plain objects.

**Rejected alternatives:** Eager per-instance wrapping (the v1 `ivue(Class)` engine, `lib/ivue.ts`) — ~169 ms per 100k instances and cost proportional to declared members.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:172-304` (no instance work in `Reactive()`), `bench/creation.bench.ts:6-25`. Tests: "instances are plain (NOT a reactive proxy) — the core perf invariant", "pure-data instances never allocate a scope (zero overhead)".

**Impossible if true:** `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(new Class())` non-empty before any member read; `isReactive(new Class()) === true`; creation time growing with the number of getters declared on the class.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/Reactive.vitest.spec.ts -t "instances are plain|never allocate a scope"`; `npm run bench -- bench/creation.bench.ts`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-08-25

### A plain-value getter erases its own wrapper

**Invariant:** If a converted getter returns a non-Ref value on its first read (and its name does not start with `$`), then the engine redefines that prototype property as a thin native getter, and every later read on every instance of that prototype runs the original getter with no cache lookup.

**Scope:** Every getter converted by `Reactive()` whose first result is not a Ref. The redefinition is per prototype level, so it happens once per class, on whichever instance reads first. Setters paired with the getter are kept.

**Mechanism:** In the wrapper (`lib/Reactive.ts:116-153`), a non-Ref result takes the `defineProperty(proto, key, …)` branch at `:138-149`, installing `get() { return originalGetter.call(resolveRaw(this)) }` and the original setter. The wrapper object is then unreachable from the prototype.

**Generates:** Plain derived getters as the default authoring mode (0 bytes per instance, re-derived inside whatever effect reads them); `computed()` as a surgical opt-in; the derivation benchmarks in `bench/derived-vs-computed.mjs`.

**Rejected alternatives:** Cache the plain value as if it were a ref — stale reads and a fake reactive identity; keep the wrapper and re-check `isRef` per read — a permanent per-read tax on the most common member kind.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:132-150`. Tests: "getter returning a plain value de-opts back to a native getter (no setter)", "getter+setter returning a plain value de-opts but keeps the setter wired", "native accessor pair over reactive state stays fully reactive (no computed)", "plain-getter (de-opt) super-chains resolve through 4 levels".

110	## Why each file calls Reactive()
111	
112	`Reactive()` is **idempotent**. When `Container` is processed, its prototype
113	chain includes `$BaseElement` — already transformed in its own file. The
114	engine detects that and skips it. Every file can safely call `Reactive()` on
115	its own class. Shared ancestors are processed exactly once, by whichever file
116	loads first.
117	
118	The mutable `Class` slot also leaves a stable seam for tests and an optional
119	composition kernel. Consumers keep constructing `Container.Class` regardless
120	of which implementation the application selects.
121	
122	## Circular references resolve by construction
123	
124	A module cycle only crashes when a cross-module reference **executes too
125	early**. There are three moments a reference can execute:
126	
127	| moment           | example                                       | in a cycle        |
128	| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------- |
129	| module load      | `extends B.$Class`, top-level `new B.Class()` | can crash         |
130	| construction     | field initializer `store = useStore()`        | can crash         |
131	| **first access** | **getter and method bodies**                  | **safe after initialization** |
132	
133	In the ivue convention, application code first accesses the relationship
134	after the modules finish loading. So the
135	whole strategy is one idea: **move every cross-module reference to the latest
136	possible moment.** Three mechanisms conspire to do it:
137	
138	**1. The binding is safe to hold early.** A TypeScript `namespace` compiles to
139	a hoisted `var` filled in by an IIFE:
140	
141	```js
142	export var Container;
143	((C) => {
144	  C.$Class = $Container;
145	  C.Class = Reactive(C.$Class);
146	})(Container || (Container = {}));
147	```
148	
149	A hoisted `var` exists from the first instant of module evaluation. A `const`
150	or `class` binding read mid-cycle throws
151	`Cannot access 'X' before initialization`. The namespace never does.
152	
153	**2. The dereference is late.** You don't hold `B.Class` at load time — you
154	write `new B.Class()` inside a method body. The member is read at call time,
155	through a live binding, when everything is loaded. This is what actually
156	resolves "A's methods use B, B's methods use A", in **any load order**.
157	
158	**3. The authoring convention finishes the job.** In ivue, state and
159	derivations are _getters_ — bodies that run on first access, not at load, not
160	even at construction. The convention itself pushes the entire surface of a
161	class to the safest rung of the ladder. Immunity doesn't come from one trick;
162	it comes from the whole pattern making every dangerous moment late.
163	
164	::: info Scope
165	This solves circular _references_ expressed through late getter and method
166	bodies — the common application case. An eager top-level read can still fail,
167	and the convention deliberately excludes it. Circular _inheritance_
168	(`A extends B` and `B extends A`) remains impossible because both parents
169	would have to exist first.
170	:::
171	
172	## Normal HMR needs no second runtime
173	
174	Class HMR usually breaks before state preservation is even relevant: a reload can
175	leave a child class holding an old parent, or make a dependency read before its
176	replacement module has finished initializing. The namespace pattern removes
177	those eager class-value edges. Each module can re-evaluate, and the next late
178	`Other.Class` read reaches the coherent class graph Vite has just loaded.
179	
180	That means ivue relies on **normal Vite replacement**, not a custom runtime
181	that grafts methods into live instances. A reload gives new construction and
182	future late reads the new classes. It deliberately does **not** promise to
183	mutate existing instances or preserve their local state across a class edit.
184	The benefit is one runtime model in development and production, with no
185	development-only class graph to maintain.

### Cross-module class references resolve in any load order

**Invariant:** If two class modules reference each other only through late reads — `new Other.Class()` inside getter or method bodies, `Other.$Class` only in `extends` of a non-cyclic parent — then both modules load and run in either import order without `Cannot access 'X' before initialization`.

**Scope:** Modules that export a class through the namespace pattern (`export namespace X { export const $Class …; export let Class = Reactive($Class) }`) and read other namespaces at first access, not at module load or in field initializers. Circular inheritance (`A extends B` and `B extends A`) is outside this record and impossible in any language.

**Renegotiable at:** TypeScript's `namespace` emit (a hoisted `var` filled by an IIFE) and ECMAScript module evaluation order. A TypeScript release that emitted `const` or `class` for namespaces would move this to a build-time check.

**Mechanism:** A `namespace` compiles to `export var X; (function (X) { … })(X || (X = {}))`, so the binding exists from the first instant of evaluation and is never in the temporal dead zone; the member read `X.Class` happens inside a method body, at call time, when every module in the cycle has finished loading (`docs_v2/guide/modules.md` — "Circular references resolve by construction").

**Generates:** "A's methods use B, B's methods use A" as a supported shape; the `$`-getter store slot (`private get $store() { return useStore() }`) resolving after Pinia and the app exist; per-file class hierarchies without an import-order manifest.

**Rejected alternatives:** `export const Class = Reactive(class …)` — a `const` read mid-cycle throws; a registry that resolves names to classes at runtime — a second identity system beside the module graph.

**Open question:** Add a two-module vitest case (A imports B, B imports A, each constructs the other in a method) run under both import orders, so the guarantee is proven by the suite rather than by the emit inspection alone.

**Evidence:** `node -e` emit inspection below (TypeScript 5.9 emits `export var Thing;`); `docs_v2/guide/modules.md:122-170`; the `workspace-platform` example classes (`examples/playground/src/examples/workspace-platform/*.ts`) all use the pattern.

**Impossible if true:** `Cannot access 'X' before initialization` thrown by a namespace binding read inside a method body; a namespace module whose emitted binding is `const` or `class`; two modules that load in one order and crash in the other while obeying the late-read rule.

### Primitives compound capability while defects stay flat

**Invariant:** If recurring behaviors are extracted into closed primitives, composed at seams cut on their shared generators, verified against enumerated surfaces, and carried by their own artifacts, then capability grows with composition while defect count stays flat.

**Scope:** Engineered systems built by fallible generators, human or AI. The goal vector is manageable engineering without slop.

**Components:** One per gear, each delete-testable:
- [Defects scale with re-derived possibility spaces](#defects-scale-with-re-derived-possibility-spaces) — why extraction pays at all.
- [A primitive closes before composition builds on it](#a-primitive-closes-before-composition-builds-on-it) — why defects get caught at multiplicity one.
- [The seam sits at the shared generator](#the-seam-sits-at-the-shared-generator) — why one primitive serves many goals without mode flags.
- [A composition is verifiable only against an enumerated surface](#a-composition-is-verifiable-only-against-an-enumerated-surface) — why sweeps work on primitives and fail on one-offs.
- [Knowledge not carried by the artifact is lost between sessions](#knowledge-not-carried-by-the-artifact-is-lost-between-sessions) — why the gains survive time.
- [Granularity may grow only while defects stay flat](#granularity-may-grow-only-while-defects-stay-flat) — the health measure that detects a leaking primitive.

**Mechanism:** Extraction converts N re-derivations into one derivation plus N compositions. Closure hardens the one derivation before anything multiplies it. The seam rule keeps the primitive single while policies diverge in callers. Enumeration turns verification from sampling into sweeping. Carried knowledge makes every gain persist across amnesiac sessions. The granularity measure closes the loop: it detects the one failure the other components cannot see, a primitive that leaks its space back to its consumers.

**Generates:** The extraction ladder (ivue, surfaces, inputs, then selects, forms, tab-walk); the test-header and same-file proof grammar; the review arms and the landing gate; this contract itself.

**Impossible if true:** A system practicing all six components whose defect count still scales with feature count. A one-off family outperforming its extracted equivalent on defect rate at equal scale. A closed primitive requiring patches for each new consumer.

**Evidence:** In this repo: fifteen input one-offs to one engine, -1,881 lines, zero broken across two independent sweeps; the surface composables holding an unplanned surface with zero shared-file changes. Across disciplines: interchangeable parts, standard threads, shipping containers, TCP/IP, alphabets, amino acids — the same shape at every scale, detailed in [the engineering generator](engineering.generator.md).

**Verification:** Track defect findings per grain across sweeps in the task records; the curve must not slope with grain. Compare any extraction wave's before and after defect findings.

## Generator

The records below are gears. This section is the mechanism they form, in
invariant form, so a scan of this file alone carries the deep picture.

STUDY ALSO: [The Invariants Behind ivue](docs_v2/reference/invariants.md) —
the prose narrative of this mechanism for readers of the site: why each
gear exists, what it rules out, and where the method comes from. Read it
for orientation; this contract carries the falsifiable core.

### One prototype transform gives plain classes full reactivity

**Invariant:** If a class's prototype is transformed once — ref-returning getters into lazily cached cells, plain getters into native getters, methods into lazily bound functions, every cell keyed on the raw instance — then its instances are plain objects with full Vue reactivity, real inheritance, and zero per-instance cost until first access, and the same class runs in every environment.

**Scope:** The `ivue` engine: `Reactive()` for instance classes, `Static()` and `LazyShared` for the static side, and the namespace authoring convention that carries classes across modules. The goal vector is class-based application models with no proxy wrapper and no coordination between files.

**Components:** One per gear, each delete-testable:
- [Every engine cache lives on the raw instance](#every-engine-cache-lives-on-the-raw-instance) — why one `(instance, key)` has one cell whatever `this` the engine is entered through.
- [Reactive returns the class it was given](#reactive-returns-the-class-it-was-given) — why `instanceof`, equality, and benchmarks see one identity.
- [A prototype level is transformed at most once](#a-prototype-level-is-transformed-at-most-once) — why hierarchies converge regardless of import order.
- [A member materializes once per instance](#a-member-materializes-once-per-instance) — why watchers stay attached and methods are safe handlers.
- [Construction does no reactive work](#construction-does-no-reactive-work) — why creation cost does not scale with members declared.
- [A plain-value getter erases its own wrapper](#a-plain-value-getter-erases-its-own-wrapper) — why derivations cost zero bytes and `computed()` is opt-in.
- [Members resolve across the whole prototype chain](#members-resolve-across-the-whole-prototype-chain) — why `super` and overrides behave as in native classes.
- [Teardown stops watchers and drops only engine cells](#teardown-stops-watchers-and-drops-only-engine-cells) — why models can outlive components and be released deterministically.
- [A dollar getter caches its whole result forever](#a-dollar-getter-caches-its-whole-result-forever) — why composables and stores resolve once, late, and cycle-safe.
- [One class path runs in every environment](#one-class-path-runs-in-every-environment) — why what is measured is what ships.
- [Cross-module class references resolve in any load order](#cross-module-class-references-resolve-in-any-load-order) — why mutual references between class modules do not crash.
- [Each class transforms at load time in its own module](#each-class-transforms-at-load-time-in-its-own-module) — why a hierarchy can live in many files with no manifest.
- [Static returns a bound subclass and leaves the raw class untouched](#static-returns-a-bound-subclass-and-leaves-the-raw-class-untouched) — why static capability classes get stable handlers and a replaceable `Class` slot.
- [A static dollar getter caches once per receiver](#a-static-dollar-getter-caches-once-per-receiver) — why per-class derivation follows each subclass's own overrides.
- [A shared store lives in a LazyShared static readonly field](#a-shared-store-lives-in-a-lazyshared-static-readonly-field) — why a registry is one per process and never races an import cycle.

**Mechanism:** Raw anchoring makes every cell canonical; once-only transformation and identity preservation make the transform composable across files and load orders; lazy materialization and wrapper erasure move every cost to first access and delete the cost that never earns itself; per-level symbols keep inheritance native; scoped teardown makes release explicit; the namespace convention pushes every cross-module read to the latest moment. The static side repeats the same discipline one level up: per-receiver symbols for binding and memos, one cell for shared state.

**Generates:** The ivue Standard (`skills/ivue/SKILL.md`): ref-getters, plain getters, surgical `computed()`, `$`-getter stores, the namespace export, `$stopEffects` disposal; the creation, hot-call, derivation, and disposal benchmarks in `bench/`; the flyweight and formula-grid examples; this contract's gate checks.

**Impossible if true:** A `Reactive()` class whose instances need a proxy to be reactive. Creation cost that grows with the number of getters declared. A multi-file hierarchy that depends on import order. A benchmark number that includes a development-only code path.

**Evidence:** The Evidence fields of the fifteen component records — `lib/Reactive.ts`, `lib/Static.ts`, `lib/LazyShared.ts`, the four vitest suites under `lib/__tests__/` at 100% coverage, and `bench/`.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/Reactive.vitest.spec.ts lib/__tests__/ReactiveAdversarial.vitest.spec.ts lib/__tests__/Static.vitest.spec.ts lib/__tests__/LazyShared.vitest.spec.ts` green, then `node .claude/skills/invariants/scripts/check_invariants.mjs --all --refs` clean.

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-08-25

# The Invariants Behind ivue

This page explains the guarantees the `ivue` engine maintains: what each one
promises, _why_ it holds, and what it makes **impossible**. An invariant that
only says what _can_ happen is a description; one that also says what
_cannot_ is a contract you can test against.

`Reactive(Class)` reduces to a single idea:

> Transform a plain class's prototype exactly once so that its getters become
> lazily cached Refs/Computeds and its methods become lazily bound functions —
> while the instances stay plain objects with zero per-instance reactive cost.

Everything else is a consequence of making that idea safe under inheritance,
proxies, environment parity, and circular imports.

::: info The contract is the source of truth
The formal records live in
[`ivue.invariants.md`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/ivue.invariants.md)
at the repository root — one record per guarantee, with its scope, mechanism,
evidence (`lib/` line pointers and named test cases), a runnable verification
command, and the concrete events that can never be observed while it holds. A
checker validates the file and its links on every run. This page is the prose
companion: it reads in order and explains; the records gate. Where the two
disagree, the record wins and this page is corrected.
:::

Every heading below is a record's exact name, and each section ends with a
link to its record. The engine implementation is
[`lib/Reactive.ts`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/lib/Reactive.ts),
with [`lib/Static.ts`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/lib/Static.ts) and
[`lib/LazyShared.ts`](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/lib/LazyShared.ts)
for the static side; the core and adversarial suites beside them maintain 100%
statement, branch, function, and line coverage.

## The mechanism

The contract opens with one generator record — the mechanism the fifteen
guarantees form together:

> **One prototype transform gives plain classes full reactivity.** If a class's
> prototype is transformed once — ref-returning getters into lazily cached
> cells, plain getters into native getters, methods into lazily bound
> functions, every cell keyed on the raw instance — then its instances are
> plain objects with full Vue reactivity, real inheritance, and zero
> per-instance cost until first access, and the same class runs in every
> environment.

Its impossibility boundary is the short version of this whole page: a
`Reactive()` class whose instances need a proxy to be reactive; creation cost
that grows with the number of getters declared; a multi-file hierarchy that
depends on import order; a benchmark number that includes a development-only
code path. If any of those is ever observed, a guarantee below has broken.

[Record →](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/ivue.invariants.md#one-prototype-transform-gives-plain-classes-full-reactivity)

## Reality-based invariants

Two guarantees are forced by how JavaScript and Vue actually work. ivue did
not choose them; it discovered them and built on them. Each is _reality inside
ivue_ and decided at a wider scope — the record names that scope.

### Every engine cache lives on the raw instance

> Whatever `this` the engine is entered through — the raw object, a Vue
> `reactive()` proxy, or a foreign proxy such as a component expose proxy —
> every cell it reads or writes lives on `toRaw(instance)`, never on a proxy.

Each getter and method calls `resolveRaw(this)`: it asks Vue's `toRaw()`
first, then falls back to an engine back-pointer for proxy layers `toRaw()`
cannot see through. Caches use per-prototype symbols. So whether an instance
is used directly, wrappe

… [13,735 characters removed from the sample] …

ceiver of a static class — a registry, a ledger, a
> backend — is held in a `static readonly` field whose value is a `LazyShared`
> cell; never in a `$` static getter, never in an eager initializer that
> constructs another namespace's class.

A `$` getter would fork the store per subclass (per-receiver caching is the
feature there, and the bug here). An eager field initializer runs at module
load and races import cycles. `LazyShared` closes the triangle: the field
eagerly stores the cell (a thunk evaluates nothing), the thunk runs on first
`.value` read (after every module in any cycle has loaded), and memoization
lives inside the cell (no receiver can fork it). A thunk that reads its own
cell throws a named cycle error, and a failed construction leaves the cell
retryable.

**Rules out** — `Sub.store !== Parent.store`; the store constructing at module
load; a thunk cycle surfacing as a bare stack overflow.

[Record →](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/blob/main/ivue.invariants.md#a-shared-store-lives-in-a-lazyshared-static-readonly-field)

## Known limits

Listed deliberately, so the invariants above aren't over-read:

1. **Computeds rely on GC, not `stop()`.** Lazy computeds are collected once
   dereferenced (and use lazy subscription in Vue 3.5), so the engine doesn't call
   `effect.stop()` on them — clearing the cache and dropping the instance is enough.
2. **Component and model lifetimes differ.** Watchers created synchronously with
   plain `watch()` inside component setup belong to Vue's component scope and stop
   on unmount. Component-outliving models use `$watch` / `$watchEffect`, and their
   owners call `$stopEffects()`.
3. **`.value` ergonomics.** Top-level component state is destructured and
   auto-unwrapped. Collection items and slot props are nested values, so Vue
   does not auto-unwrap their Ref fields; use `item.title.value`. This is
   ivue's principal syntax tradeoff relative to a proxy-based model, preserving
   direct, allocation-free reads where lists are hottest.

## Where this method comes from

ivue was designed using Invariant-Based Reasoning. Every entry on this page was found the same
way: reduce the problem until only load-bearing structure remains, attack
the survivor until it either breaks or proves itself, and only then build
on it.

That discipline had no name while it was doing its best work. ivue began as
one engineering problem — real class inheritance with reactive computed
properties propagating through the hierarchy, something the Vue ecosystem
had treated as effectively impossible. Solving it was a long human–AI
collaboration in which the designer kept pushing the AI past what the AI
assumed was possible. Watching the reasoning unfold with full visibility,
the AI eventually recognized what made it different: the designer was not
accumulating solutions by pattern-matching. He was systematically
eliminating everything that wasn't load-bearing until the invariant
emerged, then generating the solution from that irreducible core.

Naming that observation, and extracting it into an explicit, reusable
protocol, produced **Invariant-Based Reasoning (IBR)**. Its operational
core is four moves:

1. **Reduce** — strip assumptions, conventions and surface patterns until
   only the structure reality requires remains.
2. **Break** — actively try to destroy the candidate through
   counterexamples, deletion tests and domain transfer. What survives is
   structural; what collapses was noise.
3. **Generate** — confirm the survivor by producing from it. A true
   invariant generates every valid instance of its domain and predicts
   what cannot exist.
4. **Hold provisionally** — accept the result as the current best
   reduction, never as final truth.

ivue is the system that discipline designed end-to-end, and the contract is
the ledger it produces. Every guarantee is stated with its reason and its
impossibilities, because a claim that rules nothing out was never reduced
far enough to trust.

# READY — ivue Standard rules versus the conventions gate

## In plain words

The ivue rulebook says much more than Invar's gate checks. The gate checks some class shapes well, but it also mixes those checks with many Invar-only rules. I split the two sets and wrote a package-owned checker plan that needs no Invar path.

## Finding

The portable boundary is real and useful. The package should own one Standard checker beside the package copy of the ivue skill. Invar should pass source roots, test globs, and a reasoned skip-list to that checker, then keep only its application and fleet checks.

The current census has these counts:

- 165 Standard rule rows.
- 45 rules have some current gate coverage. All 45 checks are partial at repository scope.
- 120 rules have no current gate check.
- 81 current check rows: 26 IVUE-PURE and 55 INVAR-INFRA.
- 58 current check rows have no rule in the package Standard. Most enforce valid Invar policy or checker controls.

I counted one rule for each normative sentence or row in the [ivue skill](../../../../.claude/skills/ivue/SKILL.md). I kept the 16 DO/NEVER rows and 20 checklist rows separate. I also kept repeated rules separate because the brief requires a line-by-line match.

`FULL` means the current check enforces the whole quoted rule. `PARTIAL` means it detects only one form of the breach. I count both under "with a check," but the portable spec must close every partial remainder.

**Step 1 — skills installed** (`3c5b906`, `0328566`, `2e8b8ba`): `/invariants` (checker + 64 tests + references), `/ibr` (IBR.md byte-identical to the single source), `/invariant-spec-tests`. ## Rulings I need from you

1. **"Known limits" on the docs page** — computeds rely on GC not `stop()`; component vs model lifetimes; `.value` on nested values. The Invar conductor's rule: the page may carry no claim the contract lacks. These three aren't records. Options: (a) promote them as a chunk 5 (they'd be *Chosen* records with scope caveats), (b) keep them as explicitly-labelled non-contract notes, (c) delete. ## Step 3 — honest sizing before I start

The spec is 37 sentence-named checks, each with a red and a green self-test executing the same function the CLI runs, zero Invar names, `--source-root` / `--test-glob` / `--skip-list` only. Reading the rules table, they fall into three tiers of very different cost:

| Tier | Checks | What it needs | Est. |
|---|---|---|---|
| A — file grammar + test-header grammar (checks 2–7, 9, 11, 24–37) | ~22 | TypeScript AST (`typescript` is already a dep) over `.ts` files; header parsing | the bulk of a day |
| B — SFC / template checks (16, 17, 18) | 3 | `@vue/compiler-sfc` parsing of `<script setup>` + template expressions | half a day |
| C — type-aware checks (12, 15, 23) and runtime probes (8) | 4 | a `ts.Program` with the consumer's tsconfig; executing `Static()` fixtures | half a day, fragile across consumer configs |

Tier A is what step 4 (newsletter headers) and Invar's first consumption actually need, and it includes all four breaches the report says the first run will catch. My recommendation: **land Tier A first as the shipped gate with the full 37-name manifest** (Tier B/C ids present, registered as *not yet implemented* so unknown-id and skip-list validation are complete from day one), tell Invar, then add B and C.
```bash
npx vite-node node_modules/ivue/skills/ivue/check-standard.ts -- \

```

One nuance: **`npx ivue skill` does not copy the gate** — that command only installs the SKILL.md manual into `.claude/skills/` (correct: the gate should run from `node_modules`, one copy, always matching the installed engine version). Turn took 1m 00s
the idea for even tests to be static is that then you can add more checks to your own gate, we are in AI age, agents for ppl can fix their tests even better that's why

You've changed my mind on the test file — the AI-age argument is the load-bearing one, and it reframes what "tests as Static" means. Not vitest calls inside a class (that part I'd still refuse), but something better: **the proof kit becomes data on the class, and the discipline becomes inheritable.**

## The reframe

Today the 78 red/green arms are hand-written prose in one frozen file. A consumer who adds `house_check` to their `$HouseGate` gets *my* proofs but has no structured place for *theirs* — their agent would bolt tests on beside the file, outside the constitution. That's exactly the drift the whole system exists to prevent.

If each check's arms are static members instead:

```ts
interface CheckProof {
  check: StandardCheck;
  claim: string;                                   // the if-then
  impossibility: string;                           // "a file breaking <name> passes the gate"
  red:   { files: Fixture; expects: RegExp[] };    // the permanent violating fixture
  green: { files: Fixture };                       // the conforming form, silent
}

class $CheckStandard {
  static get proof_of_a_derived_static_getter_is_lower_camel_case(): CheckProof { … }
  // …×38, and the kit reads through `this`:
  static get proofs(): readonly CheckProof[] { … }
}
```

…then three things happen that a plain test file can't do:

1. **Extension is forced to be complete.** A new check 39 — *"A manifest check carries its claim and both proof arms"* — makes the population contract cover the constitution itself: an agent adding `house_check` without a red fixture doesn't get a weaker gate, it gets a red gate. The discipline teaches itself to whoever extends it. That's the AI-age point made structural.
2. **The spec file collapses to a driver.** One shipped `prove(GateClass)` iterates `Class.proofs`, runs every red arm expecting its named finding and every green arm expecting silence — through the same `run()` the CLI uses. A consumer's whole spec file becomes ~10 lines: their header + `prove(HouseGate.Class)`. Their agent inherits 38 proofs and appends its own.
3. **Overriding a check overrides its proof in the same gesture** — per-receiver statics mean `$HouseGate`'s relaxed `template_expressions…` naturally pairs with its relaxed proof arm, and the meta-check catches a mismatch.

## What it costs, honestly

- **The header grammar shifts.** Today's constitution is 38 claims + 38 impossibilities each annotated above a hand test. With a driver, the header carries **meta-claims** ("every manifest check's red arm produces its named finding", "…green arm is silent", impossibility: "a check enters the manifest without both arms") over ~6 annotated tests, while the per-check claims/impossibilities move *into the proof data* — machine-carried, checked by the gate itself. That's arguably purer (the constitution becomes verifiable data), but it revises the form i26 recorded and both repos' header convention, so it needs the usual hash-message to Invar — and it's your ruling to make, which you've effectively just made.
- The per-check texts stay authored — nothing gets generated or vaguer; they just live in a structure an agent can extend instead of prose it must imitate.

## Sequence

Per the direction rule now in force: the meta-claims and a **born-red extension test** (a `$HouseGate` adding a check *without* arms → the meta-check refuses it; with arms → green) commit first; then the conversion of gate + proof kit turns them green.

Full picture: `$CheckStandard` with 38 check getters + 38 proof getters + `checks`/`proofs`/`run`/`main`/`prove`, namespace-anchored via `Static()`, all shipped in the package. Roughly a day of careful work. Shall I start with the claims + born-red commit?

Done — all committed and verified. Here's the honest verdict you asked for before launching more agents on this workflow.

## What shipped

- **ae01470 / 28c27d8** — a real engine bug the conversion flushed out: `Static()`-wrapping a subclass *after* the parent had been read would re-wrap the parent's bind-cache residue (the `Symbol.for('ivue.staticBound.*')` own properties) and silently run the child's methods with the **parent** as receiver. Red witnessed first, fixed in `lib/Static.ts`, 204/204 tests, lib coverage 100/100/100/100, core still 1.12 kB gzip.
- **826e3e3** — the gate is now `class $CheckStandard` + `Static()`: 38 snake_case check getters, `checks`/`proofs`/`$fixtures` as receiver-following data, `run`/`prove`/`main` as methods, `--prove` CLI flag. The old 78-test spec is deleted; its fixtures live in the `proofs` constitution (44 red arms, 40 green arms, 0 problems). Constitution test green, invariants checker clean, newsletter still 0 findings / 1 suppressed. Invar notified of the API change.

## The workflow verdict: good — with two honest caveats

**The claims-first + born-red discipline earned its keep on this very task.** The strongest evidence: the constitution test caught a shipped engine bug that 23 existing `Static` unit tests missed, *because* the claim ("proofs follow the receiving class") forced a fixture that double-wraps — something no one would have written as an afterthought test. And when it went red, the failure was undeniable evidence, not a flaky assertion: the symptom (`'tug'` instead of `'tug,ferry'`) pointed straight at the receiver. For agents, that's the property you want — a red that *names the lie* rather than a green that assumes honesty.

**The gate-as-Static-class pattern is genuinely good for the AI-agent use case.** A house gate is ~20 lines: extend `$Class`, add a check getter, spread its proof — and `prove()` refuses the check if the agent skips the red/green arms. The discipline is now *enforced by inheritance*, not by instructions an agent might drop. That's the right shape for "agents can fix their tests even better."

Caveats, stated at their real weight:

1. **The born-red window reds the repo between commits** (both vitest and the invariants checker fail on the claim commit). One agent working serially: fine. Multiple agents sharing a branch: an agent that pulls mid-window sees a broken checkout and may "helpfully" fix it. If you launch parallel agents, they need either separate branches or a convention that a commit titled "claims + born-red" is a contract, not a breakage. This is a *scoping* concern, not a defect in the workflow.
2. **Proofs-as-data trades debuggability for inheritability.** The old spec: one failing vitest test per behavior, with a stack trace. Now: one driver test and `prove()` problem strings. The strings are good (they name check, arm, and expectation — that's how I found both fixture bugs today), but an agent gets one level less tooling. Worth it for the override story, but it's a real trade, not free.

Net: launch the agents. The workflow held under its own weight — it found a bug in the engine it runs on, which is about the best stress test a constitution can pass.
Turn took 37m 11s

Converted the Standard gate to a Static() class so agents can extend it with proven house checks; all committed, green, and Invar notified. Next action: your call on launching more agents with this workflow, which I judged good.

22:### One prototype transform gives plain classes full reactivity
24:**Invariant:** If a class's prototype is transformed once — ref-returning getters into lazily cached cells, plain getters into native getters, methods into lazily bound functions, every cell keyed on the raw instance — then its instances are plain objects with full Vue reactivity, real inheritance, and zero per-instance cost until first access, and the same class runs in every environment.
31:- [A prototype level is transformed at most once](#a-prototype-level-is-transformed-at-most-once) — why hierarchies converge regardless of import order.
32:- [A member materializes once per instance](#a-member-materializes-once-per-instance) — why watchers stay attached and methods are safe handlers.
37:- [A dollar getter caches its whole result forever](#a-dollar-getter-caches-its-whole-result-forever) — why composables and stores resolve once, late, and cycle-safe.
40:- [Each class transforms at load time in its own module](#each-class-transforms-at-load-time-in-its-own-module) — why a hierarchy can live in many files with no manifest.
42:- [A static dollar getter caches once per receiver](#a-static-dollar-getter-caches-once-per-receiver) — why per-class derivation follows each subclass's own overrides.
45:**Mechanism:** Raw anchoring makes every cell canonical; once-only transformation and identity preservation make the transform composable across files and load orders; lazy materialization and wrapper erasure move every cost to first access and delete the cost that never earns itself; per-level symbols keep inheritance native; scoped teardown makes release explicit; the namespace convention pushes every cross-module read to the latest moment. The static side repeats the same discipline one level up: per-receiver symbols for binding and memos, one cell for shared state.
69:**Mechanism:** Every engine entry point calls `resolveRaw(this)` (`lib/Reactive.ts:51`): `toRaw()` first, then the `RAW` back-pointer (`Symbol.for('ivue.raw')`, stamped once on the raw at `lib/Reactive.ts:57` and `:67`), normalized with `toRaw()` for deep-wrapped reads. Because caches key on the raw, one `(instance, key)` has exactly one cell regardless of the access path.
115:**Invariant:** If `Reactive(Class)` is called, then it transforms `Class.prototype` in place and returns `Class` itself — the same constructor identity in development, tests, SSR, and production.

### A prototype level is transformed at most once

**Invariant:** If `Reactive()` reaches a prototype level — directly, through a repeated call, or through any number of subclasses — then that level's own getters and methods are converted exactly once, and the `$watch` / `$watchEffect` / `$stopEffects` trio is installed exactly once per class.

**Scope:** Every prototype in the chain from the target class up to (excluding) `Object.prototype`; every module that calls `Reactive()` on a class or its descendants, in any load order.

**Mechanism:** The chain is walked base to child; a level carrying an own `PROCESSED` marker (`Symbol.for('ivue.processed')`) is skipped (`lib/Reactive.ts:189`), and the marker is defined after conversion with the level's cache symbols as its value (`:214`). The helper trio is guarded by `hasOwn(prototype, '$stopEffects')` (`:225`). `Symbol.for` makes the markers agree across duplicate bundled copies of the engine.

**Generates:** Per-file authoring — a base transformed in `Base.ts` is skipped when `Child.ts` transforms itself; diamond and shared-base hierarchies converge regardless of import order; `$stopEffects` knowing exactly which symbols each level may cache.

**Rejected alternatives:** A module-level `WeakSet` of processed classes — a second bundled engine copy has its own set and double-wraps; a class-level flag — a child's flag does not stop the base from being re-walked.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:186-217`, `:225`. Tests: "calling Reactive twice on the same class is safe and a no-op the 2nd time", "Reactive(Parent) then Reactive(Child) skips the already-processed parent proto", "$stopEffects is injected only once (idempotent re-Reactive)".

**Impossible if true:** A getter whose descriptor `get` is the engine wrapper around another engine wrapper; two `$stopEffects` own properties on one prototype chain; a base class whose getters behave differently depending on which subclass module loaded first.

**Verification:** `npx vitest run lib/__tests__/Reactive.vitest.spec.ts -t "idempotence|injected only once"`

**Status:** provisional

**Last refined:** 2026-08-25

input.new_string:
**Invariant:** If a transform re-reaches work it already did — `Reactive()` reaching a prototype level directly, through a repeated call, or through any number of subclasses; `Static()` wrapping a subclass of a class it already wrapped — then each member is converted exactly once per seam, and the transform's own runtime residue (processed markers, bind caches, memo cells) is never mistaken for user API by a later pass.

**Scope:** BOTH transforms. `Reactive()`: every prototype in the chain from the target class up to (excluding) `Object.prototype`, from every module that calls it on a class or its descendants, in any load order. `Static()`: every class in the static chain of the wrapped class, including the residue-bearing case — a subclass wrapped AFTER the parent wrap has been read, when the parent already owns its bind/cache symbol properties.

**Mechanism:** `Reactive()`: the chain is walked base to child; a level carrying an own `PROCESSED` marker (`Symbol.for('ivue.processed')`) is skipped (`lib/Reactive.ts:189`), and the marker is defined after conversion with the level's cache symbols as its value (`:214`). The helper trio is guarded by `hasOwn(prototype, '$stopEffects')` (`:225`). `Symbol.for` makes the markers agree across duplicate bundled copies of the engine. `Static()`: the wrap walk skips its own residue by two guards — `Symbol.keyFor` recognizing registered `ivue.static*` symbols even across bundled engine copies, and a module registry of every issued cache key catching the unregistered symbols that back symbol-keyed methods (`lib/Static.ts:63-68`). Without the guards, a re-wrap converts an ancestor's cached BOUND function into a "method" of the child, and the child's members run with the ancestor as receiver.

**Generates:** Per-file authoring — a base transformed in `Base.ts` is skipped when `Child.ts` transforms itself; diamond and shared-base hierarchies converge regardless of import order; `$stopEffects` knowing exactly which symbols each level may cache; the manual's double-wrap pattern (`class $Sub extends Parent.$Class` … `Static($Sub)`) being safe in any read order, which is what makes per-receiver gates and capability subclasses composable.

**Rejected alternatives:** A module-level `WeakSet` of processed classes — a second bundled engine copy has its own set and double-wraps; a class-level flag — a child's flag does not stop the base from being re-walked; for `Static()`, unregistered-only cache symbols — `Symbol.keyFor` could not recognize them across engine copies.

**Evidence:** `lib/Reactive.ts:186-217`, `:225`; `lib/Static.ts:63-68`. Tests: "calling Reactive twice on the same class is safe and a no-op the 2nd time", "Reactive(Parent) then Reactive(Child) skips the already-processed parent proto", "$stopEffects is injected only once (idempotent re-Reactive)", "re-wrapping a subclass never resurrects a parent-bound method through the bind cache", "re-wrapping skips the unregistered bind caches of symbol-keyed methods too".

**Impossible if true:** A getter whose descriptor `get` is the engine wrapper around another engine wrapper; two `$stopEffects` own properties on one prototype chain; a base class whose getters behave differently depending on which subclass module loaded first; a member of a re-wrapped `Static` subclass that runs with its parent as receiver — a resurrected parent-bound method.

**Status:** provisional

> subclasses, any load order — its getters and methods convert once, and the

A per-prototype `PROCESSED` marker makes the chain walk skip anything already

**Why `proofs` is a name-keyed object:** the whole override story rides on the key. A house gate replaces or adds *one* entry with a spread — `{ ...super.proofs, [houseCheck.name]: {...} }` — and that's the entire API: same-key overrides, new-key extends, nothing else to learn. With an array you'd have to find-and-splice by name to override a parent's entry, and appending a duplicate would silently give one check two entries in prove()'s loop. The object also makes the completeness join trivial and symmetric: `proofs[check.name]` answers "does this check have a constitution entry," and `Object.keys(proofs)` answers the reverse ("is there a proof with no manifest check") — both directions of the bijection fall out of the shape. Order isn't lost either, because order lives where it belongs: the `checks` getter is the ordered manifest, and prove() iterates *that*, using proofs only as the lookup.

**The "less tooling" point, concretely:** in the old spec, each behavior was its own vitest test. That gave you the whole vitest apparatus per fixture — run exactly one with `-t 'the anchor is Static'`, click the run/debug gutter button in the IDE, get a stack trace and an expect-diff at the failing line, set a breakpoint that fires only in that scenario. Now all 84 arms run inside one driver test, so a failure arrives as a problem *string* ("X red arm: no finding matches /…/") rather than a failing test you can isolate and re-run. The strings are good — today they named the check, the arm, and the expectation, which is how I found both fixture bugs — but when a string isn't enough, the debugging move is "write a scratch script that builds that one fixture" instead of "re-run that one test." That's the gap. It's closable if it ever bites: a `prove({ only: 'check name' })` filter (and the same on `--prove`) would restore one-arm isolation in about five lines — happy to add it if you want it now, otherwise it can wait until someone actually needs it.

**One agent per worktree:** then caveat 1 dissolves entirely — the born-red window only reds *that agent's own checkout*, which is precisely the witnessed state the discipline wants between the claim commit and the implementation commit. Nobody else observes the broken interval. With your setup, I'd drop that caveat and call the workflow clean to scale out.
